stories.headline: Trump Announces 'Biggest Oil Deal in World History' with Venezuela
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States has entered into an agreement with Venezuela granting the U.S. majority control of approximately 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves, which he described as the "biggest oil deal in world history." The deal was brokered by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Defense Department through a partnership with private business, according to the White House. Venezuelan interim president Delcy Rodríguez said the agreement would help revive her country's economy.

The agreement comes roughly nine months after U.S. forces captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges. A U.S. official said the deal would involve a partnership with a private company, with Bloomberg reporting discussions involving Venezuelan mogul Alejandro Betancourt. The arrangement is described as potentially creating the world's second-largest private oil company by reserves.

Details of the agreement's structure, timeline, and enforcement mechanisms remain unclear, with terms yet to be fully disclosed publicly. If realized, the deal would represent an unprecedented transfer of resource control from a sovereign nation to a foreign government and private partners, securing American petroleum supplies for decades, according to administration officials.

Supporters argue the deal reflects a major geopolitical and economic win, locking in vast energy resources and rewarding diplomatic pressure on the Maduro government. Critics are likely to raise questions about the legality and precedent of a foreign government taking majority control of another country's national resources, as well as the long-term stability of any arrangement tied to Venezuela's volatile political situation.

stories.headline: Greenland Cannot Conclude Whether Danish Forced Contraception Campaign Constituted Genocide, Officials Say
stories.summary:
Greenland's government said Friday it cannot determine whether Denmark's forced contraception program targeting Inuit women and girls in the 1960s and 1970s constituted genocide, after a panel of experts released two competing reports on the question. Justice Minister Marianne Paviasen told reporters the government was unable to make a definitive legal finding and called for continued public debate. A reconciliation commission will be established to address the legacy of the program.

Records show that between 1966 and 1970, approximately 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls — some as young as 13 — had intrauterine devices implanted under a Danish-administered birth-control program, often without their knowledge or consent. The widespread use of the program caused Greenland's population growth to slow markedly. Denmark issued a formal apology last August and passed legislation providing compensation of 300,000 Danish crowns (approximately $46,800) to each affected woman.

The expert panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report. The two remaining experts found that the rights of Inuit women had been violated but could not conclude genocide had occurred based on contraceptive practices alone, though they said genocidal intent remained a possible inference a court could establish based on broader evidence. The dissenting report found no evidence of intent to destroy the Greenlandic population.

The findings carry significance beyond Greenland as international debates over colonial-era policies and their legal classification continue. Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen both pledged their governments would work together on reconciliation efforts.

stories.headline: Canada Recruits Dozens of Top U.S. Researchers Amid Funding Freeze and Trade War
stories.summary:
Canada announced it is hiring 48 researchers from U.S. universities — including Harvard and the University of Michigan — as part of a C$504 million ($362 million) federal program aimed at strengthening Canadian research capacity. The move comes as the Trump administration has frozen federal research grants at numerous U.S. institutions and escalated a trade dispute with Canada. More than three-quarters of the 64 total international hires will come from the United States.

Researchers cited a deteriorating funding environment in the U.S. as a key factor in their decisions to relocate. Seth Guikema, a climate resiliency researcher formerly at the University of Michigan, said he sought opportunities abroad because U.S. funding for climate-related work had become "challenging." He will receive C$8 million over eight years to continue his research at the University of Western Ontario. Peter Caravan, a biopharmaceutical researcher who spent two decades at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital, is moving to the University of British Columbia.

Canada's Industry Minister Melanie Joly said the government was "very glad" the professors were joining Canadian institutions, and declined to characterize the hiring drive as an escalation of the trade dispute with Washington. The Trump administration has accused U.S. universities of harboring left-wing bias, promoting diversity policies it opposes, and failing to address campus antisemitism — pressure that has contributed to funding uncertainty across American academic institutions.

The talent shift raises longer-term concerns about U.S. competitiveness in scientific research, particularly in fields such as climate science, medicine, and engineering. Critics of the administration's approach to universities argue the funding freezes are accelerating a brain drain; supporters contend the moves are necessary to reform institutions they view as ideologically captured and insufficiently accountable.

stories.headline: Russian Drone Strike Kills at Least 28 Near Kyiv, Dozens Injured
stories.summary:
An overnight Russian drone assault on the Kyiv region killed at least 27 people and injured 42 others, including four children, according to regional governor Tymur Tkachenko. The strikes hit the Bucha district and prompted the evacuation of 381 residents, with search-and-rescue teams inspecting damaged buildings into Saturday morning. A separate strike in the Boryspil district killed a 14-year-old, bringing the confirmed death toll to at least 28.

President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attacks and said more than 300 emergency responders had been deployed to affected areas. The Ukrainian army reported shooting down 233 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles overnight. Zelensky also reported strikes in the regions of Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia.

Russia also reported Ukrainian strikes on the Belgorod and Rostov regions, with the Rostov governor saying seven people were injured. The exchange marks a continued intensification of drone warfare on both sides, with Kyiv increasingly targeting Russian economic infrastructure.

Zelensky appealed for additional international support and sanctions against Russia, writing on Telegram that 'Ukraine cannot be alone in finding solutions to protect against such strikes.' The mass-casualty attack is one of the deadlier single strikes on the Kyiv region in recent months.

stories.headline: RFK Jr. Alleges Pennsylvania Measles Deaths May Have Been 'Fabricated,' Escalating Feud With Governor Shapiro
stories.summary:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly suggested that two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania — including at least one newborn — may have been 'fabricated,' intensifying a public dispute with Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro over the state's handling of the outbreak. Kennedy made the claim late Wednesday; Shapiro called the statements 'inaccurate and misleading,' and the two exchanged pointed remarks both on social media and during separate press conferences.

Anti-vaccine activists have reportedly sought to contact the families of the deceased in an effort to challenge the official cause of death, drawing condemnation from public health officials. Pennsylvania state health authorities have stood by their determination that the deaths were measles-associated.

Supporters of Kennedy argue that scrutiny of public health data is legitimate, particularly given past instances of data disputes during the COVID-19 pandemic. Critics, including Shapiro and medical professionals, contend that Kennedy's claims undermine confidence in vaccination programs during an active outbreak and could fuel further spread of a preventable disease.

The confrontation is drawing national attention to ongoing tensions between the Trump administration's health leadership and state public health officials, as measles cases have risen across several states this year. A separate report indicates that documents contradict Kennedy's earlier congressional testimony about a 2019 trip to Samoa, adding pressure on the HHS secretary.

stories.headline: Thousands March on Washington on 63rd Anniversary of 1963 March, With Focus on November Midterms
stories.summary:
Thousands of demonstrators gathered on the National Mall Friday for a 'Defend the Vote' march marking the 63rd anniversary of the 1963 March on Washington, organized by Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network. Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were among the speakers who framed the rally around the November midterm elections.

Organizers pointed to a recent Supreme Court ruling that weakened a key provision of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, making it harder to challenge racially discriminatory electoral maps, as a central motivation for the march. Civil rights leaders argued that voting rights are under renewed threat and called on supporters to mobilize for the fall elections.

Republicans and conservative commentators have countered that recent changes to election law are aimed at ensuring electoral integrity rather than suppressing votes, and that Democratic messaging around voting rights is primarily an electoral mobilization tactic ahead of competitive midterms. The march drew a broad coalition of civil rights organizations, labor unions, and Democratic activists.

The event reflects heightened Democratic urgency heading into the November elections, as the party seeks to recapture congressional majorities. Speakers invoked Martin Luther King Jr.'s legacy and called the midterms a defining moment for civil rights protections.

stories.headline: CBC Reverses Guidance Barring Journalists From Calling 9/11 a 'Terrorist Attack'
stories.summary:
Canada's public broadcaster, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, reversed an internal editorial policy Friday after widespread backlash over a leaked memo that instructed journalists not to describe Al Qaeda's September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States as 'terrorist attacks.' The memo, first reported by The Toronto Sun, sparked immediate condemnation from Canadian political leaders across party lines, days before the 25th anniversary observances.

The CBC said Friday it was walking back the guidance, acknowledging the criticism. The memo had reflected a longstanding CBC editorial standard discouraging the use of the word 'terrorism' in news reporting without attribution, a policy the broadcaster has maintained to avoid what it described as value-laden language — a rationale that critics found inapplicable to the 9/11 attacks.

The reversal came after politicians and commentators called the guidance an example of overcorrection in journalistic neutrality standards. The incident has reignited a broader debate in Canada and internationally about the appropriate boundaries of editorial restraint when describing events widely regarded as acts of mass-casualty terrorism.

The CBC's about-face ahead of the approaching anniversary of the attacks underscores the political sensitivity of the issue and the speed with which internal media policies can become public controversies in the social media era.
